hotspots.text: The seven-pronged trident crowning the prang, the Trident of Shiva the Destroyer, like the ear of a corn stalk against the sky.
hotspots.title: The trident

hotspots.text: The Khmer tiers recede as they rise, a mountain in masonry. The prang symbolizes Mount Meru, the center of the universe, and the five towers evoke the thirty-three heavens.
hotspots.title: A mountain in masonry

hotspots.text: The skin is broken Chinese porcelain, once ballast in trading ships, set with Mauritia mauritiana shells. In the morning light it shines with a pearly iridescence.
hotspots.title: Ballast porcelain

hotspots.text: Indra, god of lightning and cloud, rides the three-headed royal elephant Erawan above the upper terrace.
hotspots.title: Indra on Erawan

hotspots.title: The steep stairs

hotspots.text: The Ordination Hall's Niramitr Buddha was said to have been designed by Rama II himself, and his ashes rest in the image's base.
hotspots.title: The Niramitr Buddha

intro: On the west bank of the Chao Phraya rises a tower skinned in broken Chinese porcelain that glows at dawn. This is Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, rebuilt by kings into Bangkok's most recognizable silhouette.
page_title: Wat Arun: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: The temple is older than Bangkok. It stood in the Ayutthaya period as Wat Makok, the Olive Temple. When King Taksin made Thonburi his capital after Ayutthaya's fall, he renamed it Wat Chaeng, the Temple of Dawn, and it briefly housed the Emerald Buddha before the image moved across the river to Wat Phra Kaew in 1784. The name honors Aruna, the Hindu god of the dawn, and the temple has faced the sunrise over the river ever since.
sections.heading: Older than Bangkok

sections.body: The tower that defines the skyline came in the early 19th century. Rama II renamed the temple Wat Arunratchatharam, restored it, and began enlarging the central prang from a modest 16-meter shrine into a Khmer-style mountain. His successor Rama III finished the work in 1851, raising it to about 80 meters and sheathing it in the porcelain mosaics that give the temple its pearly shine. Rama IV later gave the temple its present full name, Wat Arunratchawararam. The prang's exact height is reported anywhere from 66.8 to 86 meters, but nobody disputes what it is: the tallest riverside structure of its age, which no one dared to match for fear it would tilt into the river.
sections.heading: Two kings raise a mountain

sections.body: Look closely and the tower is a mosaic made of garbage. Chinese trading ships arrived in Bangkok with tons of porcelain ballast and left it behind; temple builders broke it up and set the shards into the prang in floral patterns, mixed with shells. Around the base stand figures of ancient Chinese soldiers and animals, and over the second terrace ride four statues of Indra on Erawan. The Ordination Hall holds the Niramitr Buddha, designed by Rama II himself, with murals from the reign of Rama V. At the riverside, six Chinese-style pavilions of green granite hold the landing bridges where the ferries still dock.
sections.heading: Porcelain, shells and elephants

sections.body: Wat Arun is one of Bangkok's most filmed landmarks, and filmmakers come for the stairs. Mortal Kombat (2021) staged a fight sequence on the prang's famously steep steps, using the climb itself as drama. The Korean drama King the Land (2023) used the temple's sunset silhouette as a romantic backdrop, the porcelain tower glowing over the river at the golden hour. Directors return to it for the same reason painters and photographers do: from across the Chao Phraya, the prang is Bangkok in a single vertical line, instantly readable anywhere in the world.
